summary.title: Securing Rails Applications
summary.one_liner: You learn how Rails handles authentication, session storage and hijacking, session fixation, and CSRF, plus the countermeasures for each.
takeaways: Rails 8.0+ ships an authentication generator that adds sessions, password reset, and bcrypt-hashed passwords, but you must still build sign-up yourself.
Session hijacking is countered by forcing SSL (config.force_ssl = true), offering a prominent log-out button, and keeping secrets long and random.
CookieStore sessions are encrypted but can be replayed; keep sensitive or changing data like credits in the database instead of the session.
Call reset_session after a successful login to defeat session fixation, and expire sessions server-side with a timestamp sweep.
CSRF happens when a crafted link or image triggers requests with the victim's cookie; use GET and POST correctly and add security tokens to non-GET requests.
summary.summary: This Rails Guides chapter covers web application security with a focus on Rails. It starts with the authentication generator introduced in Rails 8.0, showing the files it creates, how has_secure_password and authenticate_by work, and how session management is structured. It then explains sessions, including session hijacking, CookieStore storage limits, replay attacks, session fixation with its countermeasures, and server-side session expiry. The page ends with an introduction to cross-site request forgery (CSRF) and the start of its countermeasures; the text is cut off before the CSRF countermeasure details are complete. The guide is example-driven, with code snippets, shell output, and attack walkthroughs.
